title: My Home Recording Setup for Guitar
text: [music] [music] >> So, I've had a lot of requests in the comment section recently to demonstrate how I record guitars here at my home studio. So, today let's walk through some of the gear I use and demonstrate some sounds. To give a broad overview, my guitar goes into a pedal board and then into an amp which is mic'd with two microphones that run into a pair of API mic pre's um that then go into my Universal Audio Apollo. And that connects to the computer. Now, the recording software I use here is Luna and I monitor everything through a pair of Yamaha monitors. Now, the guitars change from video to video as you guys know, um but everything else here stays set up pretty much the same. So, let's talk about some of the specific gear, how I like to set things, and as we go we'll kind of demonstrate some sounds. So, today I'm playing my Danocaster Tele which has a set of throwback pickups in it. And this is running into my studio board. This is a bigger board that pretty much stays here at the studio full time. And uh this board's got a bunch of stuff on it. Um but really what we're going to talk about today specifically is the pedals, the few pedals that I use day-to-day when I'm making videos, which is these two overdrive pedals, the Roger Mayer Voodoo 1 and the Analog Man King of Tone, and then we'll talk about the delay, which I I use a lot, the Boss Delay Machine. Now, this board runs out to an old um mid-60s Fender Princeton Reverb, which has an Eminence speaker in it. Um let's start out by just demonstrating the sound of this guitar on the neck pickup straight into the amp. Now, the amp's got um a little bit of reverb on it and it's set pretty clean. So, here's what the straight amp sounds like with no effects. >> [music] >> So, that's how I like to set an amp generally, um whether it's in the studio or live because it gives you a really nice platform to start adding pedals and effects, and it kind of works equally well with every guitar. Um so, the first kind of thing I would add to that would be a little bit of delay using this Boss Delay Machine. And the way I like to set my delay is to have three, maybe four repeats that kind of die out and get a little bit dark as they go, and maybe with a slight bit of modulation. But, here's um a basic delay sound. So, you can hear there's two, maybe three repeats. Um you know, I might set it a little bit more intense than that for a certain thing. Um but, that's kind of a nice general delay. Kind of stays out of the way. >> [music] >> Of course, I could lean down and turn up the effect volume a little bit if I want more ambience. And then you can hear more of those repeats. >> [music] >> And this delay has a tap tempo, which is really handy. So, depending on the tempo of the song, um I can tap it in if I want a faster delay. You know, I get that kind of almost slap-backy thing. I can set it much longer and get a really nice long ambient delay. >> [music] >> Now, from here I'll start adding some overdrives. Um that's going to add a little bit of compression to the sound and also a little bit of grit and character. Um this first overdrive I use the Roger Mayer Voodoo One. Um I set it kind of like a boost. It adds a little bit of hair. It honestly in a track still kind of reads as clean. But, it's nice for certain types of clean sounds where you want a little bit more character and grit. So, here's the Voodoo One. Here it is off first. >> [music] >> And then here it is on. Right? So, it adds a little bit of body and just a little bit of hair, but still reads as clean. >> [music] [music] >> As you dig in, it starts to break up a little bit. >> [music] >> But really expressive and really nice. I use that sound a lot in videos um for bluesier stuff where I don't want really a really overdriven sound, but I want a little bit of character and a little bit of compression. Um the next stage of gain I'll use will be the red side of the King of Tone, the Analog Man King of Tone. So, I'll turn that Voodoo One off and here's the clean sound again. And then here's the red side of the King of Tone. So, this is a little bit more obvious overdrive pedal kind of sound. >> [music] [music] >> Um now, if I want a little bit more than that, um I'll stack those two sounds together. So, here's the >> [music] >> King of Tone by itself. Now, when I put the Voodoo One on in front of it, you get more of that low-end uh body from the Voodoo One and um you know, a little bit of extra push of that boost going into the King of Tone. >> [music] >> So, >> [music] [music] [music] >> Right, so a really nice and expressive sound. Sorry, I lost the switch tip on my Tele the other day at a gig, so it's a little bit difficult to switch the pickups here. >> [music] >> There's the neck pickup. If I go to the middle, >> [music] >> that nice quacky middle sound. And then the bridge. >> [music] [music] >> So, that's kind of the pedal board sounds that I use sometimes in videos for rhythm. I may click on this Boss tremolo. You [music] hear me use that sometimes. The other sounds I have on here um this Arion chorus, which I rarely use, honestly. >> [music] >> Um that's kind [singing] of a slow chorus sound. >> [music] >> Sometimes I'll set it faster for a faux Leslie thing. Something like this. >> [music] >> Uh which is a nice sound. And then I have this Yard Box fuzz, which is kind of like a fuzz distortion, which honestly I don't know if I've ever used in a video here on this channel, but sometimes on sessions uh I'll use this sound um often times I'll stack it just in front of my overdrive sound. >> [music] [music] [music] >> Not a sound I use a lot, but that's a great pedal. Those old Yard Box pedals are, uh, kind of hard to find, but very cool. Um, so now let's talk about the amp settings. Um, I have a bunch of amps here at the studio, but for recording I almost exclusively use my old Princeton Reverb, which is in a little room, basically behind the camera right over there. Um, it's not a heavily treated room, but it just isolates the amp a little bit from where I'm sitting. Um, and then that's miked with two mics, um, a Shure SM57 and a Royer 121 ribbon mic. So, I'm going to play a little bit and then I'll go in and I'll solo, um, the two mics, um, so you can kind of hear what they each sound like. I'll play this first. I'll go back to a cleaner sound. This is just the Voodoo One. Let's see. >> [music] >> Little delay, a little Voodoo One. So, this kind of sound, which I use a lot. Here's what the 57 sounds like on its own. >> [music] [music] >> All right, so here's what the Royer now sounds like on its own. It's a much darker sound. I'll try to play a similar thing here to uh give you a little comparison. >> [music] [music] >> So, those two sounds combined together really nicely. The warmer uh fuller sound of the Royer ribbon mic combined with the more focused mid-rangey harsher sound of the 57, which really cuts through the mix. Um and yeah, basically I just kind of positioned those a little bit off the center of the cone of the speaker, back an inch or two off the grill cloth. Basically, just move it around until it sounds good. I don't really think about it too much. Um and then those mic mics run into these API preamps behind me, which are basically just set kind of you know, it depends on the guitar you're playing and how loud the amp is, um how much actual volume the mics are getting hit with. I may tweak it a little bit if I switch to a guitar with hotter pickups or if I change settings on the amp. Um but basically, I just set the preamps right until they're, you know, not clipping. So, as loud as they can get without hitting the red and starting to get some of that harsh distortion. Uh but basically, you want to, you know, hit your recording software, your you know, the computer with as much signal as possible. That's going to give you a nice loud full sound um that's really going to sit in the track the best. So, here's the sound of these two mics combined together now. >> [music] [music] [music] >> So, a really rich and beautiful sound. Now, when I'm doing lessons here, as you guys know, I create backing tracks. Um, most of the backing tracks I've done in the studio with real musicians. Um, uh, we've done a lot of tracks over at my friend Wes Little's studio. And, you know, it's live tracking with a band, keyboards, bass, drums. And we record everything, and then I bring the files back here, load them up on the computer, and can record my guitars here for the video lessons. Um, so, you know, that's pretty easy. You just kind of drag and drop those tracks into the session you're working on, and then I play my guitar and film it on the video, and edit it all together. So, that's kind of the process here, and that's a little bit of a walk-through of the the gear. Now, one thing I will add, there's a couple plugins that I use, um, on my master bus, um, when I'm making tracks. So, I don't usually do any kind of processing on the guitar with EQs or compression or any kind of plugins on the actual guitar tracks, but I do put some, um, kind of mastering compression on the actual master bus for the whole track. And mostly that's just to ensure that the tracks really um cut well um in the video. I mean, when you're watching a video on computer speakers or on a phone, um a lot of the nuance and details can get lost, so it's nice to have uh the track recorded really loud and kind of mastered so that you can hear everything and it really stands out. So, um in Luna, I use the API summing um plug-in and I use the API bus compressor. Um I just kind of use some general default settings and just kind of set it uh in a subtle way to sound nice. I also use the Waves um SSL bus compressor and I use the Waves uh 1073 uh plug-in in the mid-side uh setting that just kind of widens everything out and gives everything a little bit of space. Um but those are the basic plug-ins I use. It's nothing fancy. Uh I'm certainly not an expert on mixing or mastering. Um but those are just the ones that I've found that work. So, when you hear the guitar sitting in the track, there's sort of that glue-like compression and uh a little bit of that spatial stuff to kind of tie everything together to make it sit in the track really well. So, that's something to be aware of when you're recording guitar at home. But essentially, it's a pretty simple formula. Uh good guitar, couple of good pedals, a great old amp, um and then miked with that classic combination of mics. You know, using a couple of good mics and really using good mic preamps does make a huge difference. Um I've done it without the mic preamps and there's a noticeable difference when you have that good analog hardware in the mix. Um and then just a good uh interface like the the Apollo. And then just using your ear to match the volume, set the compression, um and get everything sitting nicely in the mix. So, that's how I do it. So, hopefully this is helpful for those of you that are out there doing home recording of your own and have asked about my particular sounds that I get here. All right, guys. Until next time, happy practicing and take care.
